title: Refugees
objective: After this level you can explain refugees and the right to asylum.
summary: Nansen's 1922 passport helped refugees with no country. The 1951 Convention defines refugees and forbids returning them to danger. Most displaced people stay inside their country.

cards.headline: In 1922, a polar explorer created a passport for people with no country.
cards.body: In 1921 the League of Nations made Fridtjof Nansen its first High Commissioner for Refugees, to help people fleeing Russia after the revolution. Many had lost their nationality. His "Nansen passport" let them travel to other countries to look for work; about 450,000 people used one. Nansen received the Nobel Peace Prize in 1922.

cards.headline: Who counts as a refugee
cards.body: Today's rule comes from the 1951 Refugee Convention. A refugee is someone outside their own country who can't or won't return to its protection because of a well-founded fear of being persecuted for their race, religion, nationality, membership of a particular social group or political opinion. And UNHCR says refugee status is declaratory: you're a refugee from the moment you meet the criteria, before any official says so.

cards.fact: The core rule: no sending refugees back into danger.
cards.context: It's called non-refoulement. Article 33 of the 1951 Convention says a refugee must not be expelled or returned to a territory where their life or freedom would be threatened, and UNHCR calls it one of the most fundamental principles of international law. Asylum is the protection a state grants to someone fleeing persecution or serious harm, and UNHCR says seeking it is a human right.

cards.fact: Most people forced from home never cross a border.
cards.context: UNHCR's Global Trends report counted 117.8 million people forcibly displaced at the end of 2025. Of them, 41.6 million were refugees and 68.7 million were displaced inside their own countries. Because the 1951 definition requires being outside your own country, those 68.7 million aren't refugees in law, even though they fled home too.

cards.headline: Refugees: protected
learned: Nansen's 1922 passport helped people with no country
1951 Convention: outside your country, fearing persecution

questions.prompt: What did the Nansen passport of 1922 give refugees who had lost their nationality?

options.label: Automatic citizenship in Norway
options.rationale: It was a travel document, not citizenship.

options.label: A travel document for seeking work abroad
A free passage home to Russia
options.rationale: It helped them travel onward to find work, not go back.

options.label: A seat in the League of Nations
options.rationale: Individuals didn't get seats; states did.

questions.explanation: The Nansen passport let refugees who had lost their nationality travel to other countries to look for work.

questions.prompt: What does the principle of non-refoulement forbid?

options.label: Granting asylum to more than one family member
options.rationale: It says nothing about family size.

options.label: Refugees working in their host country
options.rationale: It's about sending people back, not work.

options.label: Countries sharing refugee data with the UN
Returning refugees to where their life or freedom is threatened

questions.explanation: Under Article 33 of the 1951 Convention, a refugee must not be expelled or returned to a territory where their life or freedom would be threatened.

questions.prompt: Level 19's Fragile States Index counts refugees and internally displaced people. What separates the two under the 1951 Convention?

options.label: Refugees fled danger; displaced people didn't
options.rationale: Both fled home; the difference is the border.

options.label: Refugees are outside their own country
Displaced people have lost their nationality
options.rationale: It's about staying inside the country, not nationality.

options.label: Only refugees are counted by UNHCR

questions.explanation: The 1951 definition requires being outside your own country, so people displaced inside it aren't refugees in law, though both fled home.
